pr_title: [Fix #13501] Add new cop `StructUnnecessaryKeywordInit` to check for unnecessary `keyword_init: true` in Struct.new
pr_body:
Fix #13501

This pull request introduces a new RuboCop cop to check for unnecessary `keyword_init: true` in `Struct.new` and includes the necessary configurations, implementation, and tests.

### New Cop Implementation:

* Added `Style/StructUnnecessaryKeywordInit` cop to check for unnecessary `keyword_init: true` in `Struct.new` in `config/default.yml`.
* Implemented the `StructUnnecessaryKeywordInit` cop in `lib/rubocop/cop/style/struct_unnecessary_keyword_init.rb`, which detects and autocorrects instances where `keyword_init: true` is used unnecessarily.
* Required the new cop in `lib/rubocop.rb` to ensure it is loaded.

### Testing:

* Added tests for the new cop in `spec/rubocop/cop/style/struct_unnecessary_keyword_init_spec.rb` to verify it correctly identifies and autocorrects offenses, and to ensure it does not flag acceptable uses of `Struct.new`.

-----------------

* [x] Wrote [good commit messages][1].
* [x] Commit message starts with `[Fix #issue-number]` (if the related issue exists).
* [x] Feature branch is up-to-date with `master` (if not - rebase it).
* [x] Squashed related commits together.
* [x] Added tests.
* [x] Ran `bundle exec rake default`. It executes all tests and runs RuboCop on its own code.
* [x] Added an entry (file) to the [changelog folder](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/master/changelog/) named `{change_type}_{change_description}.md` if the new code introduces user-observable changes. See [changelog entry format](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#changelog-entry-format) for details.

pr_comments: Usually it's not a bad idea to add submit a matching rule to the Ruby Style Guide as well, so it's easier for people to understand why a cop exists.

It is an edge case, but it would be prudent to consider scenarios where multiple `keyword_init` keyword arguments are specified.  

e.g.,  

```ruby
Struct.new(:foo, keyword_init: true, keyword_init: false)
Struct.new(:foo, keyword_init: true, keyword_init: true)
Struct.new(:foo, keyword_init: false, keyword_init: true)
```

issue_context.title: Lint for redundant keyword_init on structs
issue_context.body:
## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Ruby 3.2 enables keyword_init on structs without specifying it. https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2022/12/25/ruby-3-2-0-released/

```rb
# before 3.2
foo = Struct.new(:bar, keyword_init: true)

# equivalent after 3.2
foo = Struct.new(:bar)
```

## Describe the solution you'd like

A lint for redundant keyword_init: true on structs.
comments:
This change introduces a behavioral incompatibility with the `Struct.keyword_init?` method, so it may be worth considering whether "redundant" is an appropriate designation.

```ruby
Struct.new(:bar, keyword_init: true).keyword_init? # => true
Struct.new(:bar).keyword_init? # => nil
```

Good catch @koic!
Do you think that behaviour makes sense for the `keyword_init?` method? 

The default has changed. Consumers relying on `!Struct.new(:bar).keyword_init?` will not be aware of the change. I'm not sure what the patterns usually are for `?` methods in Ruby. However, I think in my experience, the expectation is that `nil` will be treated as falsy rather than truth-y for `?` methods.

Yeah, RuboCop is used widely across applications, libraries, and frameworks, and user programs can include unexpected cases. Rather than focusing on whether it is a predicate method, it is important to consider the potentials for altering existing behavior, which differs from layout changes.

OK that makes sense.

> consider the potentials for altering existing behavior, which differs from layout changes.

Would it make sense to have the cop disabled by default with the safety warning that `keyword_init?` doesn't respond the same when using keyword_init explicitly?
Technically, for Ruby 3.2+, it seems possible to pending it by default with `SafeAutoCorrect: false`.
This issue has been automatically marked as stale because it has not had any recent activity. It will be closed soon if no further activity occurs. Thank you for your contribution and understanding!

This is an easy one to implement and I think it makes sense. I'd like to keep this open for now.

Only for >= 3.2 makes sense. Here's the feature request for ruby for adding `keyword_init?` method: https://bugs.ruby-lang.org/issues/18008. Making it unafe seems ok but I can't imagine it mattering much.

Ref https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/pull/13893#discussion_r1966495970

Should this be closed? I learned that `keyword_init: true` does more than the name suggests, and also blocks initialization with positional arguments entirely.

Is this something to care about? I think, most add `keyword_init: true` to stay compatible with older ruby versions.

review_comments:
Strictly following the behavior, the default value of `keyword_init` is `nil`, not `true`. The difference in their behavior needs to be considered.

```console
$ ruby -e 'p Struct.new.keyword_init?'
nil
$ ruby -e 'p Struct.new(keyword_init: nil).keyword_init?'
nil
$ ruby -e 'p Struct.new(keyword_init: true).keyword_init?'
true
$ ruby -e 'p Struct.new(keyword_init: false).keyword_init?'
false
```

For more details, please refer to the documentation:
https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/master/Struct.html#method-c-new

> **Keyword Argument**
>
> By default, the arguments for initializing an instance of the new subclass can be both positional and keyword arguments.
>
> Optional keyword argument keyword_init: allows to force only one type of arguments to be accepted:
>
> ```ruby
> KeywordsOnly = Struct.new(:foo, :bar, keyword_init: true)
> KeywordsOnly.new(bar: 1, foo: 0)
> # => #<struct KeywordsOnly foo=0, bar=1>
> KeywordsOnly.new(0, 1)
> # Raises ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments
>
> PositionalOnly = Struct.new(:foo, :bar, keyword_init: false)
> PositionalOnly.new(0, 1)
> # => #<struct PositionalOnly foo=0, bar=1>
> PositionalOnly.new(bar: 1, foo: 0)
> # => #<struct PositionalOnly foo={:foo=>1, :bar=>2}, bar=nil>
> # Note that no error is raised, but arguments treated as one hash value
>
> # Same as not providing keyword_init:
> Any = Struct.new(:foo, :bar, keyword_init: nil)
> Any.new(foo: 1, bar: 2)
> # => #<struct Any foo=1, bar=2>
> Any.new(1, 2)
> # => #<struct Any foo=1, bar=2>
> ```
Thank you for the detailed explanation.
Indeed, after looking into it, removing `keyword_init: true` doesn't make sense.
`keyword_init: true` isn't redundant at all, but actually a required keyword argument.

Should I close this PR?
Is my understanding correct that `keyword_init: nil` would be considered redundant writing/syntax?
